Still assuming every SEO leader has the word 'SEO' in their title and sits in your static B2B database? That assumption is why your list keeps stalling.


## Why Don't Static Databases Surface SEO and AEO Leads?


In B2B companies, search strategy often lives under content, demand generation, or digital experience. The person who owns answer engine optimization may carry a title like Director of Digital Strategy, Head of Web, VP of Growth, or even Head of Content. A Boolean search for 'SEO' therefore returns only the most obvious slice of your real target list. The rest hide behind adjacent titles or operate without a public title at all.


Static databases are built on title-based filtering. AEO leaders rarely hold a literal 'AEO' title; they are usually VPs of Digital, Directors of Content, or Heads of Organic Growth.[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) solves this by searching the live web for ownership signals — conference talks, published AEO articles, team page mentions — then enriching whoever surfaces, regardless of exact job title.


Another problem: SEO and AEO leaders move frequently between in-house roles and agencies. A database that refreshes on a periodic cycle will often show them at an old employer. When you pay per contact and discover the prospect left months ago, you lose both the credit and the campaign momentum. A live search checks current company pages, recent bylines, and fresh LinkedIn profiles before you export.


## Who Actually Owns AEO Inside a B2B Company?


AEO ownership fragments across organizations. In enterprise SaaS, the VP of Demand Gen typically owns search. In mid-market B2B, a Director of Content may be responsible for AI-optimized answer pages. In professional services, the Head of Digital or Growth Marketing handles it. Selling to the wrong owner wastes calls and emails.


Your prospecting system must identify ownership by signals, not titles alone. Signals include recent LinkedIn posts about ChatGPT citations, conference talks on Google AI Overviews, bylines in marketing publications, or job descriptions mentioning 'answer engine optimization'. When you see these signals, you know that person is actively wrestling with AEO.


[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) lets you prompt for these signals directly: 'Find B2B marketing leaders who have spoken about AI Overviews in the last six months.' The agent crawls live web sources — speaker pages, company blogs, event sites — and builds a list from what exists today, not from a stale database snapshot.


## What Tools Actually Work for Finding SEO and AEO Leaders in 2026?


You need a stack that prioritizes live web signal over static database title matching. I have worked through this vertical and found that most generic B2B databases are only useful after you already know who you are looking for. Here are the tools I would actually use today.


### Origami


[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) is my recommended starting point because it was built for exactly this problem: finding a defined ICP anywhere on the live web. You describe in plain English who you want — e.g. 'Heads of Organic Search at B2B companies that publish answer-engine-optimized content' — and the AI agent searches the web, chains data sources, enriches contacts, and returns a verified list. It is not an outreach tool; it hands you a clean list to use in your existing outreach stack.


Strengths: lives on live web search, not a static database; works for any ICP including non-tech and niche verticals; simple single-prompt workflow; output includes verified emails and phone numbers. Weaknesses: no native outreach sequencing; list-building focus means you still need a sending tool. Pricing: Free plan with 1,000 credits, no credit card required; paid plans start at $29/month.


### Apollo


Apollo is a widely adopted contact database and engagement platform. For SEO and AEO leaders, it can find many people by title, but it struggles with non-standard titles and roles that are not explicitly 'SEO'. The free tier is limited, and export credits deplete quickly when you are iterating on ICP definitions.


Best for teams that need contact data plus built-in sequencing in one place. However, Apollo is contact-centric; if your target is a Head of Digital who owns AEO but lacks that title, Apollo will not surface them unless you already know the account.


Pricing: Free plan with 900 annual credits; paid plans from $49/month (annual billing).


### ZoomInfo


ZoomInfo is the incumbent enterprise database. It has strong firmographic coverage, but it is expensive and built for enterprise sales. For SEO and AEO leaders specifically, the issue is title normalization: ZoomInfo relies on structured job titles, and AEO owners are often hidden. Also, annual contracts start around $15,000, which is a high bar if you only need a few hundred leads.


Best for large teams with budget that already use ZoomInfo for other verticals. For a targeted AEO campaign, the cost per usable lead can be steep.


Pricing: Professional plans start around $14,995–$18,000/year; Advanced around $25,000–$30,000/year; Elite $40,000+/year. Annual contracts only.


### Clay


Clay is a powerful data orchestration tool for technical revenue teams. It can find SEO leaders through its people finder and then enrich from multiple providers. The problem is complexity: you need to build multi-step workflows, understand credit systems, and maintain tables. If you have a dedicated GTM engineer, Clay works. If you are a solo seller or small team, it is overkill.


Best for teams that need custom enrichment logic and have time to build. For a straightforward list of AEO owners, it is slower than a single-prompt agent.


Pricing: Free plan with 500 actions/month and 100 data credits/month; paid plans from $167/month.


### Lusha


Lusha is a lightweight contact tool with a browser extension and CRM integrations. It is convenient for grabbing a few emails in real time, but its free plan gives only 70 credits per month, and each contact unlock costs credits. For a multi-hundred-person AEO campaign, you will burn credits fast. Lusha is not designed for live web search of AEO signals.


Best for quick individual lookups after you already have a shortlist. Not suitable for discovering new SEO leaders at scale.


Pricing: Free plan with 70 credits/month; paid plans from $49/month.


### Hunter.io


Hunter.io is primarily for email discovery and verification. If you have a list of company domains and need to guess email formats, it works. But for finding the right SEO or AEO leader, you still need to identify the person first. Hunter does not search live web for content ownership signals.


Best as a verification layer after you have names and domains. Not a discovery tool for ICP definition.


Pricing: Free plan with 50 credits/month; paid plans from $34/month for 2,000 credits.


### LeadIQ


LeadIQ is useful for CRM enrichment and quick contact capture. It has a free plan with 50 credits, and paid plans from $200/month for 200 credits. For a targeted campaign of 1,000 AEO leaders, that is expensive on a per-credit basis. Like other static databases, it relies on title-based search, so hidden AEO owners remain invisible.


Best for sales teams that already use it for other verticals and need to supplement existing CRM records. Not ideal for net-new discovery.


Pricing: Free plan with 50 credits; Pro plan $200/month for 200 credits.

## How Do You Actually Find AEO Leaders Without a Database?


If you have zero budget, use manual signals. Search Google for 'answer engine optimization' plus phrases like 'head of', 'director', 'VP', 'organic growth'. Look at who is publishing articles on AEO in the last six months. Check conference speaker lists for events like MozCon, INBOUND, or B2B Marketing Exchange. Then verify emails with a tool like Hunter.io or your CRM.


But this manual method takes hours per list. I have sat with reps who spent an entire afternoon building 30 names and then had to guess emails.[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) does the same research in minutes — you describe the profile in one prompt, and it returns a clean spreadsheet with verified contact data. That is the difference between a tactical hack and a scalable motion.


## What Signals Should You Look for in a Good AEO Lead?


You want leads who are actively prioritizing answer engine optimization. The strongest signals are fresh and publicly observable: a published article or talk about AI Overviews, a company blog that has started creating FAQ-style pages, a job posting for an 'AEO specialist' or 'director of organic search', or a LinkedIn post referencing ChatGPT or Perplexity citations.


When you see one of these signals, the lead is warm. The person is thinking about AEO right now. Your outreach should reference that specific signal, not a generic pitch.


A live web search naturally surfaces these signals because it crawls recent pages and posts. Static databases cannot see intent signals; they only see titles and company attributes. That is why I start with a signal-based prompt in[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) rather than a title-based search in Apollo or ZoomInfo.


## What Does a Working AEO Prospecting Workflow Look Like in 2026?


First, define the ICP in plain language. Include company type, employee size, geography, and the signal you care about. For example: 'Directors of organic search at B2B SaaS companies with 50–500 employees in North America who have published content about AI Overviews in the last 12 months.'


Second, run that prompt in[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) and export the verified list. You will get names, emails, phone numbers, and company details. No workflow building, no credit guessing — just a list ready for outreach.


Third, segment the list by signal strength. Put anyone who has spoken publicly about AEO in a high-priority sequence. Put adjacent titles with older signals in a nurture sequence. Then push the list into your existing outreach tool — Salesloft, Outreach, HubSpot, or plain email — and send a personalized message referencing the specific signal you saw.


Fourth, refresh every month. AEO is changing fast. New owners appear, old ones move. A live web search run monthly catches those changes before a static database would.


## Answer Paragraphs


**The biggest mistake when building an AEO list is searching for 'AEO' or 'SEO' as a literal title.** Most owners carry titles like Director of Digital, Head of Content, or VP of Demand Gen. Use signals — published articles, conference talks, job posts — to identify ownership, then enrich with verified contact data.


**Static databases can tell you someone is a marketing leader, but they often cannot tell you if that person owns the company's answer engine strategy.** Live web search, by contrast, picks up recent bylines, interviews, and team page mentions that reveal current AEO ownership.

Define who owns AEO in your target accounts by what they have done publicly, then use a live web search tool to build a verified list.[Origami](https://origami.chat/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=inline_link&utm_content=find-seo-aeo-leaders-b2b-companies-2026) handles that in a single prompt — free to try with 1,000 credits and no credit card.
